name: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
title: Social Hierarchy of the Haudenosaunee: From Clan Mother to Captive
period: 1609–1779 (from the start of the Beaver Wars to the Sullivan Expedition)

tiers.name: Clan mothers
tiers.you: As an elder woman of your clan, you choose its chief and can take the antlers of office from him if he fails his people; when a family grieves, you can demand that the warriors go out for captives.
tiers.kid: Clan mothers were respected older women who chose the chiefs of their clans and could remove them.
tiers.rise: The clan mothers were the elder women of their clans, held in high regard as those who had raised children; leadership passed within the clan’s female line.
tiers.why: The clan mothers, the elder women of each clan, chose its chiefs.

tiers.name: League chiefs
tiers.you: Your clan’s women chose you, and you gave up your own name for a chief’s title; you sit in council seeking agreement with the other chiefs, and if you fail your people the clan mother can take your antlers away.
tiers.kid: Fifty chiefs met in the Grand Council of the League, and they had to agree before acting together.
tiers.rise: Clan mothers chose a chief from his clan and could remove him, when he gave up the title and took his old name again. In 1687 the French seized fifty chiefs under a flag of truce and shipped them to Marseille as galley slaves; 13 came back in 1689.
tiers.why: The League’s Grand Council was an assembly of fifty chiefs (royaner), each representing a clan of a nation.

tiers.name: Pine tree chiefs and war chiefs
tiers.you: You lead war parties and speak for your nation abroad, but in the Grand Council you only watch and carry messages: you have no vote there.
tiers.kid: War chiefs led war parties, and other chiefs travelled as messengers to talk with other nations.
tiers.rise: No birthright made a war chief: valour in war was a prerequisite for any man to be made a chief, and patronage counted, as Molly Brant’s did when her brother Joseph became a war chief.
tiers.why: Below the League chiefs stood two kinds of leader who could not vote in council: the pine tree chiefs, who served as diplomats, and the war chiefs, who led the war parties.

tiers.name: Faithkeepers and healers
tiers.you: Appointed by the elders, you keep the ceremonies of the year, from the Maple festival to Midwinter, and on the great days a society’s masked dancers drive sickness away.
tiers.kid: Faithkeepers, both men and women, led the festivals that gave thanks for maple sap, strawberries and corn.
tiers.rise: Faithkeepers were appointed by the elders and took names reserved for their office; the medicine societies admitted members by initiation, at first, it seems, by moiety.
tiers.why: Faithkeepers are part-time specialists who conduct the religious ceremonies.

tiers.name: Warriors
tiers.you: You go out with a small war party to bring back captives for a grieving family; a captive is worth more than a scalp, and losing one of your own would undo the raid.
tiers.kid: Young men went to war to prove their courage, often to bring back captives rather than to kill.
tiers.rise: Every man could become a warrior; renown in war opened the way to a chief’s title, while cowardice, branded by the clan mothers, left a man unmarriageable.
tiers.why: War was a young man’s road to standing.

tiers.name: The people of the longhouse
tiers.you: You belong to your mother’s clan and live in its longhouse with other families; the women plant and harvest the Three Sisters, the men hunt and go to war, and no one owns the land.
tiers.kid: Families lived in long bark houses; women grew corn, beans and squash, and children belonged to their mother’s clan.
tiers.rise: One was born into one’s mother’s clan. Outsiders entered by adoption, and at marriage a young couple lived in the longhouse of the wife’s family.
tiers.why: Most people lived in palisaded villages that Europeans called castles, one to four for each nation at a time, moved every five to twenty years as soil and firewood ran out.

tiers.name: Adopted captives
tiers.you: Taken in a raid, you were beaten, burned and renamed, and now you live in the place of a dead member of your adoptive family; if you prove yourself, you will be one of them.
tiers.kid: Captives taken in war were often adopted into families to take the place of people who had died.
tiers.rise: Capture and adoption brought people here; an adoptee who lived up to the dead person’s place could rise with it, and in time many became full members, while one who resisted or fled could be killed.
tiers.why: The mourning wars brought captives into the villages to replace the dead.

tiers.name: Captives kept as slaves
tiers.you: You were taken in a raid and not adopted: you work at the village’s tasks, may be traded away, and the word for you is the word for a domestic animal.
tiers.kid: Some captives were not adopted and had to work for the village, or were traded away.
tiers.rise: War, ransom or a family’s choice put a captive here; adoption was the way out, and a captive who resisted could be killed. Once European settlers brought African slavery to North America, some Haudenosaunee, such as Joseph Brant, owned enslaved Africans.
